extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in political history, criminal justice, press freedom, and 18th-century social commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts from 18th-century political and social essays/letters (Benjamin Franklin and contemporaries) addressing freedom of speech, criminal law, trade policy, poor relief, and customs. The text mixes historical narrative, legal argument, and moral/political prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of speech is essential to a free constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: "To suppress inquiries into the administration is good policy in an arbitrary government; but a free constitution and freedom of speech have such reciprocal dependance on each other, that they cannot subsist without consisting together."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues that censorship and suppression of inquiry are tools of arbitrary power and that a free constitution depends on permitting public inquiry and criticism. Anti-pattern: using prosecutions or licensing to intimidate public discussion (examples: prosecutions in Star Chamber, licensers for stage and press).

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of laws that punish mere words; requirement of overt act for treason
rubrics_metrics.description: Case of Sidney: defence that private writings or 'imagining' are not overt acts of treason — "Scribere et publicare est agere" vs. "Scribere est agere" — and the warning that "a judge, by remote inferences and distant innuendoes, may construe the most innocent expressions into capital crimes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: penal statutes should not criminalize unmanifested thoughts or private writings; publication or some overt act is needed before treating expression as criminal. Anti-pattern: judges treating 'known principles' or private notes as sufficient evidence of treason (example: Sidney's conviction despite lack of publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of punishments to offences
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Frenchman is for proportioning punishments to offences." "That it is better a hundred guilty persons should escape than that one innocent person should suffer, is a maxim..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishments should not exceed the moral and legal gravity of the offence. Example: criticizes capital punishment for petty theft (woman capitally convicted for gauze worth fourteen shillings and threepence). Scoring guidance: laws should be examined for proportionality; severe penalties for minor property crimes are condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment beyond the merit of the offence is punishment of innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: "To put a man to death for an offence which does not deserve death, is it not a murder?... Is not all punishment inflicted beyond the merit of the offence, so much punishment of innocence?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral-legal standard: penal systems that mete out excessive punishment commit injustice comparable to harming the innocent. Use historical examples (Old Bailey case) to illustrate the social scale of such injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive/deterrent justifications must not override justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of the reasoning that harsh punishments for property crimes are justified so "that horses may not be stolen." The author rejects using disproportionate severity simply as a preventive tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should not accept arguments that deterrence alone justifies disproportionate penalties. Anti-pattern: invoking 'prevention of crimes' to justify extreme punishments without regard to equity or proportionality (Judge Burnet's reply cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing and censorship of stage/press corrupt public morals
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of a licenser for the stage and press who encouraged plays that 'debase the minds of the people' and turned comedy into indecency; contrast with writers (Steele and Addison) who 'rescued the stage' and recommended amiable, rational characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative claim: the censoring influence of a licenser can be used to promote vice and debase public taste; a free, uncensored press/stage can restore virtue by allowing truth and critique to triumph. Anti-pattern: state-directed licensure producing obscene or politically propagandistic works that attack civic institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public poor relief should promote self-reliance, avoid creating dependency
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that "the more public provisions were made for the poor, the less they provided for themselves... the less was done for them, the more they did for themselves, and became richer." The author asserts public provisions have offered a premium for idleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy standard: structure poor relief to encourage industry and frugality (leading/driving people out of poverty), rather than creating permanent dependence. Example recommendation: repeal laws that remove the inducement to industry; contrast with abundant hospitals/alms leading to increased idleness in England (observations cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade policy and prohibitions must be consistent and not impose partial burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of prohibitions on export (corn, wool) that lower farmers' returns while benefiting manufacturers: "If it be a good principle that the exportation of a commodity is to be restrained...stick to that principle, and go thorough stitch with it." Questions why farmers alone should bear a partial tax to maintain cheapness for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic-policy criterion: apply trade restrictions consistently or compensate those harmed; avoid selective policies that function as hidden taxes on a particular class (farmers). Example: prohibition of wool export reduces incentive to raise sheep and then complaints about scarcity of mutton; call for indemnification if government acts illegally.
